title: NCB Flags Rising Chemsex Trend Among Indian Youth, Urges Parents to Stay Alert
excerpt: India's Narcotics Control Bureau has issued a nationwide warning about the growing practice of combining recreational drugs with sexual activity among young people, calling on parents and educators to watch for warning signs.
body:
• The Narcotics Control Bureau has flagged a rise in "chemsex" — the deliberate use of drugs such as methamphetamine, mephedrone, and GHB to enhance sexual encounters — among Indian youth.
  • The NCB warning highlights growing online chatter about chemsex on social media and dating apps, which are being used to arrange drug-fuelled meetups.
  • An AIIMS-Delhi study found that about one-third of surveyed participants reported engaging in chemsex, with meth and its variants the most commonly used substances.
  • Health experts warn the trend carries severe risks including HIV and STI transmission, overdose, addiction, and serious mental health consequences.

India's Narcotics Control Bureau has issued a nationwide alert about the growing prevalence of "chemsex" among the country's youth, warning that social media platforms and dating apps are increasingly being used to organise drug-fuelled sexual encounters. The agency has urged parents, educators, and community leaders to remain vigilant for signs of substance misuse linked to sexual activity.

Chemsex refers to the intentional use of psychoactive substances — primarily methamphetamine (crystal meth), mephedrone (known on the street as "meow meow"), and GHB/GBL — before or during sexual encounters to lower inhibitions, heighten sensations, and extend the duration of sessions. While the practice has historically been documented among men who have sex with men in Western countries, the NCB's warning signals its widening reach across demographics in India, including younger and heterosexual populations in urban areas.

Online Chatter and Dating App Networks

The NCB has flagged a spike in online conversations about chemsex on social media, messaging platforms, and dating applications, according to reports by ANI News and The Statesman. The bureau has raised concerns that dating apps are being used not only for social connections but also to arrange drug meetups, with users employing coded language and symbols to signal the availability of substances.

This aligns with findings from the NCB's Annual Report 2025, released earlier this year by Union Home Minister Amit Shah, which identified Telegram, WhatsApp, and Signal as major channels for drug distribution. The report noted that public Telegram channels operate like e-commerce platforms for narcotics, listing products, prices, and delivery details, while encrypted messaging makes enforcement particularly challenging.

In 2025, Chennai Police sought a ban on the dating app Grindr after investigations revealed it was being used as a communication channel for methamphetamine peddling, according to The New Indian Express. Officers found that dealers identified themselves through coded symbols on their profiles.

What the Research Shows

A peer-reviewed study published in the Indian Journal of Psychiatry by researchers at AIIMS, New Delhi, found that among 136 surveyed participants, 33.8% reported engaging in chemsex. Methamphetamine and its variants — marketed as "meth," "yaba," or "ice" — were the most commonly used substances, followed by MDMA, poppers, and cocaine. Nearly 46% of those practising chemsex also engaged in "slamsex," or injection drug use during sexual activity.

Separately, a case study published in the Journal of Psychosexual Health documented chemsex behaviour in a 20-year-old male college student from an urban background in Ahmedabad, noting the link between compulsive cocaine use and sexual behaviour. The researchers called for routine screening for sexualised substance use in young patients and warned that chemsex "emerges as a marker of complex emotional dysregulation, maladaptive coping, and trauma."

"Multifaceted harm reduction strategies, such as peer-based interventions, online psycho-education, and mindful programs, have demonstrated encouraging outcomes in high-risk and resistant populations."

— Journal of Psychosexual Health, 2025

Health Risks and the Broader Drug Crackdown

Health experts describe chemsex as carrying a cascade of risks. The combination of drug-impaired judgement and sexual activity significantly raises the probability of HIV and sexually transmitted infections, with studies showing those engaged in chemsex are up to 12.5 times more likely to experience sexual violence. Substances like GHB carry narrow margins between a recreational dose and a potentially fatal one, while methamphetamine use is associated with psychosis, cardiovascular damage, and rapid onset addiction.

The NCB's chemsex alert comes amid a broader government crackdown on drug-related threats. The Centre recently declared 2-Bromo-4-Methylpropiophenone — a key precursor chemical used in manufacturing mephedrone — a controlled substance under the NDPS Act, with a compliance deadline of September 7, 2026. The Drugs Controller General of India has also ordered a separate crackdown on the illegal sale of sexual enhancement medicines, citing their unregulated sale to younger people.

According to the NCB's annual report, law enforcement agencies registered over 1.48 lakh drug cases and seized more than 1,200 tonnes of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances in the reporting period.

What Parents Should Watch For

The NCB has urged parents to look for behavioural changes that may signal involvement in chemsex, including sudden shifts in social circles, unexplained absences, secretive phone use, and signs of substance use such as rapid weight loss or erratic sleep patterns. The bureau has also encouraged communities to report drug-related activity through the MANAS national narcotics helpline at 1933.

Experts say addressing chemsex in India will require moving beyond a purely enforcement-led approach. The AIIMS researchers emphasised the need for culturally appropriate harm reduction models, digital literacy programs, and treatment frameworks that respect patient confidentiality — crucial for a population often deterred from seeking help by stigma. With the practice gaining a foothold among younger demographics outside the traditionally studied MSM community, the window for early intervention is narrowing.
